newsitem.title: UK: Dollar buoyed in late Europe by strong US assets.
newsitem.headline: Dollar buoyed in late Europe by strong US assets.

text.p: Strength in U.S. stocks and bonds lifted the dollar to a fresh 37-month high against the mark in Europe's afternoon, while it was also buoyant against the yen although it was turned firmly back at around 126.50.

The dollar dipped briefly after U.S. consumer price data, the highlight of the day, turned out to be lower than expected. But this sign of mild inflation drove up U.S. Treasuries and the Dow, which gave dollar bulls ample encouragement.
Dollar/mark rallied to 1.7375, its highest since March 1994, although profit-taking kicked in later to take it slightly lower by late European trade.

The dollar was at 1.7320/30 marks at 1534 GMT compared with 1.7258/64 in late European trade on Monday. Against the yen, it was trading around the middle of the session's range at 126.26/31 against 126.42/47 yesterday.
With the market having mostly priced in another rise in key U.S. rates in the near future, its attention for the moment was on the performance of U.S. stocks and bonds, analysts said.

"While this (speculation of higher U.S. rates) is a bullish factor for the dollar, in the short-term people will be looking at the assets markets' response," said Claudio Demolli, foreign exchange analyst at Merrill Lynch here.

The market had been particularly nervous ahead of today's consumer price data because operators vividly remembered the scare on Friday, when U.S. Treasuries and the Dow were hit by higher-than-expected U.S. producer price inflation.
Today's data revealed headline CPI and core prices edged up 0.1 and 0.2 percent respectively -- both at the lower end of market expectations -- against rises of 0.3 and 0.2 in February.

"Even with good price reports, people are still convinced that inflation is a problem in the U.S. and that they will see inflation creeping up," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

While the U.S. interest rate scenario also made the dollar bullish against the yen today, lingering worries about intervention by Japanese authorities made traders steer clear of testing the 127-yen level.
But this was not much of a deterrent, particularly as the general perception was that any intervention would be carried out solo by the Bank of Japan, analysts said.

"The main risk for the dollar now is central bank intervention. But so far there hasn't been any, and without guidance from central banks, the market will probably continue to push dollar/yen higher," DMG's Lewis said.

Meanwhile, the dollar was also supported against the mark by a report by the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner to the European Central Bank, which expressed serious concerns that many European states have not managed to control their budget deficits enough to launch European monetary union in 1999.

Analysts said the EMI report was perceived as increasing the likelihood that EMU will be broad-based with softer conditions for qualification. This was particularly because of the recent strengthening in European leaders' political will to launch the project on time, which became apparent at an EU ministers' meeting earlier this month, they said.

"EMI doesn't have great perceived powers at this stage... but the report gave the market another kick in that direction after EMU sentiment became positive after the Ecofin (EU ministers') meeting," Merrill's Demolli said.

Elsewhere, the British pound rose to a fresh 4-1/2 year high of 2.8231 marks on general mark weakness, although it had backed down to 2.8193/03 by late European trade compared with Monday's 2.7965/74.
